bottom_line.headline: Democrats are favored to take the House
bottom_line.detail: Generic ballot D+8.6 (Silver Bulletin, Oct 14); RealClearPolling D+7.9. Cook projects a Democratic gain of 9–19 seats with 21 toss-ups.

bottom_line.headline: The Senate is a coin flip tilting Democratic
bottom_line.detail: Dems need net +4. Six GOP-held seats are toss-ups: Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Alaska. Polling averages have the Democrat ahead in five and Kansas tied. Markets put a Democratic Senate at 62–64%.

bottom_line.headline: Trump is deeply underwater
bottom_line.detail: Net approval −21 (RealClearPolling) to −22 (Silver Bulletin); Pew has approval at 30%, comparable to the low point of his first term.

bottom_line.headline: Hochul is comfortably ahead in New York
bottom_line.detail: Up 11–12 on Blakeman (Marist, Emerson) and 9 in Siena's last poll. One small text-message poll this week had it at 3; treat it as an outlier until a major pollster agrees.

bottom_line.headline: Buffalo and Long Island House seats are settled; NY-17 isn't

bottom_line.detail: North Tonawanda, Orchard Park, Scottsville, Dunkirk and Fredonia — Congress, state legislature, county seats and the one proposition (NT's $18M community center). Early voting Oct 24–Nov 1.

what_changed: Iowa: Marist (Oct 8–11) has Turek 48–45, the second straight poll with the Democrat ahead after YouGov's 47–46; RealClearPolling's average is now Turek +0.9. The four pickups still run through Maine, Ohio and Texas plus one of Iowa, Kansas and Alaska — and Iowa just got a little easier.

Kansas: RealClearPolling's average lands on an exact tie, 45.8–45.8. The polls showing Hamilton ahead (InsiderAdvantage +1, YouGov +3) are offset by NYT/Siena (Marshall +1) and a September co/efficient poll (Marshall +5). Still a toss-up either way.
Ohio: the average is Brown +3.1, but a Republican-leaning co/efficient poll (Oct 5–6) has Husted up 1, the first poll with Husted ahead since June. CNN's Brown +6 remains the latest nonpartisan read.

Minnesota: KSTP/SurveyUSA (Oct 15) has Flanagan 45–42 over Tafoya for the open Democratic seat; RealClearPolling counts it a toss-up, Cook Likely D. It is a hold Democrats cannot afford to lose on the way to 51.

New York: a Pollfinity text-message poll (Oct 8–12, 499 RV) has Hochul 47–44, far below Marist's 11 and Emerson's 12. The firm is self-funded by a 2024 Libertarian presidential candidate and the sample is small; the averages barely moved. Cook also moved NY-04 (Gillen) from Lean D to Likely D on Oct 9.
Generic ballot: Silver Bulletin slipped from D+8.8 to D+8.6; RealClearPolling from D+8.1 to D+7.9. Trump's approval is unchanged at −21.3 (RCP).

glossary.text: A poll question that names no candidates: "Would you vote for the Democrat or the Republican for Congress in your district?" Averaged nationally, it is the best single read on which way the House is leaning. D +9 means Democrats lead by about 9 points. For scale, 2018's blue wave was about D +8 and Democrats gained 41 seats; 2022 was roughly R +3 and Republicans barely took the House.
The share of adults who approve of the president minus the share who disapprove. Negative means more people disapprove. Presidents with net approval this low usually lose seats in a midterm.

Race ratings from the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan handicapper. Toss Up means either side could win; Lean is a slight edge; Likely a clear one; Solid is not in doubt. Ratings move when polls or candidates change.

Prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi) let people bet real money on outcomes; the price is the crowd's probability. 64% means the market thinks Democrats win the Senate about two times in three. It is a forecast, not a poll.

The Senate is 53 Republicans to 47 Democrats (counting two independents who vote with Democrats). Democrats need a net gain of four seats for 51. With Georgia, Michigan and Minnesota to defend, that means winning four of the six Republican-held toss-ups — Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Alaska.

The headline number for each Senate race is RealClearPolling's average of recent polls, which is steadier than any single survey. The note under it lists the latest individual polls. "Republican-leaning" or "Democratic-leaning" after a pollster means the firm works for that party or has a record of tilting that way — weigh those lighter.

Every poll is a sample. A typical one is accurate to about 3–5 points either way, so a 2-point lead is a coin flip and even a 6-point lead can flip. Averages of several polls are steadier than any one poll.

In the Senate section the bar runs from the middle: blue to the left for a Democratic lead, red to the right for a Republican one, longer for a bigger lead. In the governor section the two bars run toward each other and the gap is undecided voters.

outlook.title: What could still change this
outlook.lede: The October surprise already happened, in February: the Iran war. It is the main reason the president's net approval sits near −21 instead of the −10 range he held at New Year's, and nothing in the next three weeks is likely to swing the national mood that far again. So the question is not whether a shock changes the House — at D+8.6 that would take a very large one — but whether anything tips the four to six Senate seats sitting inside the margin of error.

items.why: A ceasefire, a major casualty event or an escalation is the one thing that could move national numbers several points in either direction. Everything else is small by comparison.
Gas is the number voters feel directly. A spike in the last two weeks hurts the party in power; a drop helps a little.
Texas and Maine are within two points, so one bad week for a candidate — a scandal, a debate stumble — can decide a seat.
Early voting starts Oct 24. The first week's turnout in the toss-up states is the first real signal; prediction markets react to it before the polls do.

outlook.noise: What usually matters less than it looks: a late rally blitz (it fires up both bases) and any single surprising poll. Ignore it unless an average moves.

how_to_read.title: How to read this without panicking
items: A lead of 2 points is a tie. A lead of 5 is a real edge, not a lock. Polls miss by 3–5 points in a normal year.
One poll means almost nothing. The averages on this page are what to watch, and they move slowly on purpose.
Headlines say "Democrats worry" because worry gets clicks. Check it against the numbers below before you believe it.
What would actually be bad news: the averages moving 3 or more points toward Republicans across several states at once. One state wobbling is noise.
The Senate may not be known on election night (see Election night, below). A slow count is not a bad count.

election_night.title: What to expect on election night
election_night.intro: Polls close in waves; counts finish on each state's own schedule. Here is what is normal, so a slow result doesn't read as a bad one.

items.what: New York (governor, NY-17, NY-26 and the local races) and most of the East count fast. North Carolina, Georgia and Ohio usually report the bulk of their vote within a few hours of polls closing.
Texas, Iowa and Kansas typically have near-complete counts by midnight Eastern. Michigan and Minnesota can run into the early morning when close.

Maine: if nobody clears 50% of first choices (write-in candidates make that likely), the ranked-choice count happens in Augusta and took about nine days in June's primary. Alaska: by law the ranked-choice tabulation is Nov 18 and by-mail ballots count if postmarked by Nov 3, so a close race there waits two weeks.
If the Senate comes down to Maine or Alaska, control may not be known until mid-November. That is the calendar, not a sign anything went wrong.
